SECTION: How we did this (Pages 4-5)

TOPICS: methodology, survey design, sampling, weighting, definitions, terminology

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The study was conducted by the Pew Research Center to understand Hispanic political identity and views on the 2022 midterm elections (Page 4)
- A total of 7,647 U.S. adults were surveyed, including 3,029 Hispanics, from Aug. 1-14, 2022 (Page 4)
- The sample included 1,407 Hispanic adults on the American Trends Panel (ATP) and 1,622 on Ipsos' KnowledgePanel (Page 4)
- Respondents were recruited via national, random sampling of residential addresses to ensure representativeness (Page 4)
- The data is weighted to match the U.S. Hispanic adult population by age, gender, education, nativity, and Hispanic origin group (Page 4)
- Links are provided for the survey questions, responses, and methodology (Page 4)
- The terms Hispanic and Latino are used interchangeably (Page 5)
- U.S. born refers to people who are U.S. citizens at birth, including those born in the 50 states, D.C., Puerto Rico, or other U.S. territories, as well as those born abroad to at least one U.S. citizen parent (Page 5)
- Foreign born refers to persons born outside the U.S. to parents who were not U.S. citizens; this term is used interchangeably with immigrant (Page 5)
- Second generation refers to people born in the U.S. with at least one immigrant parent (Page 5)
- Third or higher generation refers to people born in the U.S. with both parents born in the U.S. (Page 5)
- Language dominance is a composite measure based on self-described speaking and reading abilities (Page 5)
- Spanish-dominant people are more proficient in Spanish than in English (Page 5)
- Bilingual refers to people proficient in both English and Spanish (Page 5)
- English-dominant people are more proficient in English than in Spanish (Page 5)
- Respondents are considered registered voters if they self-report being absolutely certain they are registered at their current address (Page 5)
- Respondents are considered not registered to vote if they report not being registered or express uncertainty (Page 5)
- Democrat refers to respondents who identify politically with the Democratic Party (Page 5)
- Republican refers to respondents who identify politically with the Republican Party (Page 5)
- Ind/Other refers to respondents who identify politically as independent or with some other party (Page 5)

- Foreign born refers to persons born outside the U.S. to parents who were not U.S. citizens; this term is used interchangeably with immigrant. (Page 5)
- Second generation refers to people born in the U.S. with at least one immigrant parent. (Page 5)
- Third or higher generation refers to people born in the U.S. with both parents born in the U.S. (Page 5)
- Language dominance is a composite measure based on self-described speaking and reading abilities. (Page 5)

- Respondents are considered registered voters if they self-report being absolutely certain they are registered at their current address. (Page 5)

- Republican refers to respondents who identify politically with the Republican Party. (Page 5)
- Ind/Other refers to respondents who identify politically as independent or with some other party. (Page 5)

- Income tiers were created using 2020 family incomes adjusted for purchasing power by geographic region and household size. (Page 6)

- In August 2018, the ATP switched from telephone to address-based recruitment using the U.S. Postal Service's Delivery Sequence File (Page 101)
- Across three surveys, 19,718 adults were invited to join the ATP, with 9,942 (50%) agreeing to participate (Page 101)
- Across four address-based recruitments, 19,822 adults were invited, of whom 17,472 agreed to join and completed an initial profile survey (Page 101)
- Of the 27,414 individuals who have ever joined the ATP, 11,651 remained active panelists (Page 101)
- The U.S. Postal Service's Delivery Sequence File is estimated to cover up to 98% of the population (Page 101)
- The overall target population was noninstitutionalized persons ages 18 and older living in the U.S., including Alaska and Hawaii (Page 101)
- Hispanic, Asian, Black adults, and 18- to 29-year-old Republicans and Republican-leaning independents were selected with certainty (Page 101)
- The ATP was supplemented with an oversample of self-identified Hispanic respondents from the KnowledgePanel who were of Mexican origin, Central American ancestry or who had no more than a high school education (Page 102)
- The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with Ipsos (Page 102)
- The web program was rigorously tested on both PC and mobile devices by the Ipsos project management team and Pew Research Center researchers (Page 102)
- Incentive amounts ranged from $5 to $20 depending on whether the respondent belongs to a part of the population that is harder or easier to reach (Page 102)
- During the last few days of data collection, KnowledgePanel members were offered 10,000 points (equivalent to $10) in addition to the regular incentive program (Page 102)
- The data collection field period for this survey was Aug. 1-14, 2022 (Page 102)
- Invitations were sent out in two separate launches: Soft Launch and Full Launch (Page 102)
- Sixty ATP panelists and 909 KnowledgePanel (KP) panelists were included in the Soft Launch (Page 102)
- All remaining English- and Spanish-speaking panelists were included in the Full Launch and received an invitation on Aug. 3, 2022 (Page 103)
- All panelists with an email address received an email invitation and up to four email reminders if they did not respond (Page 103)
- All ATP panelists that consented to SMS messages received an SMS invitation and up to four SMS reminders (Page 103)
- As a result of data quality checks, 12 ATP and seven KP respondents were removed from the dataset prior to weighting and analysis (Page 103)
- The data was weighted in a multistep process accounting for multiple stages of sampling and nonresponse (Page 103)
- Respondents were placed into one of five sample groups based on Hispanic origin and education level (Page 103)
- Weights were calibrated to align with population benchmarks identified in the accompanying table (Page 104)
- Weights were trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles to reduce loss in precision from variance (Page 104)
- Some benchmarks come from surveys prior to February 2020; most ATP members' variables were measured in 2022 (Page 104)
- Voter registration is calculated using procedures from Hur, Achen (2013) and rescaled to include the total U.S. adult population (Page 104)
- Volunteerism is weighted to an estimated benchmark accounting for possible behavior changes since the pre-pandemic period (Page 105)
- The weighting parameter uses the 2021 volunteerism profile variable but is weighted with the 2020 profile variable (Page 105)
- For American Trends panelists recruited in 2021, the 2020 volunteerism measure was imputed using data from existing panelists with similar characteristics (Page 105)
- The survey includes an oversample of Hispanic, Asian, Black adults, and 18- to 29-year-old Republican respondents (Page 105)

It studies politics and policy; news habits and media; the internet and technology; religion; race and ethnicity; international affairs; social, demographic and economic trends; science; research methodology and data science; and immigration and migration. Pew Research Center is a subsidiary of The Pew Charitable Trusts, its primary funder.

Recruiting panelists by phone or mail ensures that nearly all U.S. adults have a chance of selection. This gives us confidence that any sample can represent the whole population, or in this case the whole U.S. Hispanic population. (See our "Methods 101" explainer on random sampling for more details.)

To further ensure the survey reflects a balanced cross-section of the nation's Hispanic adults, the data is weighted to match the U.S. Hispanic adult population by age, gender, education, nativity, Hispanic origin group and other categories. In 2022, nearly 35 million Latinos will be eligible to vote, accounting for  $14\%$  of the nation's eligible voters. The views of Latino voters have received widespread news coverage leading up to the 2022 midterm elections.[1] Overall,  $77\%$  of Latino registered voters are dissatisfied with the way things are going in the country and  $54\%$  disapprove of the way Joe Biden is handling his job as president. Meanwhile, just  $30\%$  have given "a lot of thought" to this year's congressional elections, with Latino Republicans and Republican leaners more likely than Latino Democrats and Democratic leaners to say this  $(36\%)$  vs.  $27\%$ . Yet equal shares of Latino Democrats and Democratic-leaning registered voters  $(60\%)$  and Latino Republicans and GOP-leaning registered voters  $(60\%)$  say it really matters who wins control of Congress.

Latinos' views of Biden As the midterm elections approach, fewer than half of Latino registered voters (45%) say they approve of the way Biden is handling his job as president, while about half (54%) disapprove. U.S. registered voters overall have a more negative view of Biden (61% disapprove vs. 37% approve), according to the same August survey.3 Biden's approval rating varies some across demographic subgroups of Hispanic registered voters. Hispanic Democrats hold largely positive views of Biden. Nearly two-thirds of Hispanic Democrats and Democratic leaners (65%) approve of the president's job performance, but a substantial Hispanic registered voters have mixed views of Biden $\%$  of registered voters who of the way Joe Biden is handling his job as president PEW RESEARCH CENTER minority (34%) disapprove. This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings on Latinos' views regarding abortion, gun policy, and LGBTQ rights, comparing them to U.S. adults overall. It highlights that while Latinos are divided along party lines on these issues, their views are sometimes less polarized than those of the general U.S. public. The data shows that 57% of Hispanics believe abortion should be legal in at least some cases, with significant differences between Democratic (69%) and Republican (39%) leaners. In contrast, a greater share of U.S. adults (62%) hold this view. The page also includes two bar charts: one showing abortion legality preferences by group and another comparing priorities for gun control versus gun rights. The source is a National Survey of Latinos conducted August 1-14, 2022, and a survey of U.S. adults conducted June 27-July 4, 2022.

- 39% of Hispanic Republicans and GOP leaners support abortion being legal in all or most cases.
- 62% of U.S. adults overall say abortion should be legal in at least some cases.
- 84% of U.S. adult Democrats and Democratic leaners support abortion being legal in at least some cases.
- The Supreme Court's decisions have restricted access to legal abortions and expanded rights to carry guns in public.
- High-profile mass shootings occurred in Texas and New York, leading to expanded gun rights.

This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings from a national survey of Latinos conducted August 1-14, 2022, on Hispanics' views of socialism and capitalism. The main content is a bar chart titled "About half of Hispanics have a negative impression of socialism," which breaks down the percentage of respondents with positive or negative impressions by demographic groups including political affiliation, age, and the importance of being Hispanic. The text explains that while 53% of all Hispanics have a negative impression of socialism compared to 41% with a positive one, they hold a more favorable view of capitalism (54% positive vs. 41% negative). The data shows significant partisan divides, with Hispanic Democrats split on socialism but Hispanic Republicans overwhelmingly viewing it negatively.

**Text Evidence:**
- A larger share of Hispanics have a negative (53%) than positive (41%) impression of socialism.
- Hispanics have a more positive (54%) than negative (41%) view of capitalism.
- Hispanic Democrats and Democratic leaners are split on socialism (48% negative vs. 50% positive).
- Nearly three-quarters (72%) of Hispanic Republicans and Republican leaners have a negative impression of socialism.
- The survey was conducted Aug. 1-14, 2022.

The main finding is that a majority of Hispanics (72%) view the U.S. as one of the greatest countries globally, with 51% placing it among the best and 21% believing it stands above all others. The data reveals significant differences by political affiliation and age, with Latino Democrats more likely to believe other countries are better than the U.S. (30%) compared to Republicans (18%), while older adults are less likely to hold this view. - 51% of Latinos say the U.S. is one of the greatest countries in the world along with some others.

- 26% of Latinos say there are other countries that are better than the U.S.
- 30% of Latino Democrats/Lean Dem say other countries are better than the U.S., compared to 18% of Latino Republicans/Lean Rep.
- 43% of Hispanics ages 18-29 say other countries are better than the U.S., compared to 7% of those 65+.
- 22% of Latinos say being Latino is extremely or very important.

However, it notes that Latino partisans' positive feelings for their own party are relatively lukewarm compared to their strong negative feelings toward the opposing party. The content is presented in a single section with no visual elements.

- Hispanics view the Democratic Party as more concerned about Hispanics and their interests.
- Hispanics are more likely to say Democrats work hard to earn Hispanic votes than Republicans.
- Positive feelings Latino partisans have for their own party are relatively lukewarm compared to strong negative feelings toward the opposing party.

pages.ocr_text: 2. Hispanics' views on key issues facing the nation On some key national issues, views among Hispanics are diverse and varied, and sometimes distinct from other Americans' attitudes. For example, most Hispanics say abortion should be legal in all or most cases, but views vary across religious and age groups. And on guns, Hispanics favor controlling gun ownership at higher rates than the general public. These findings come after the Supreme Court recently made major decisions on cases that resulted in restricted access to legal abortions and expanded rights to carry guns in public. When it comes to immigration, a majority of Hispanics say it is a very important policy goal to create a path to legal status for immigrants who arrived illegally to the U.S. as children – a greater share than among the U.S. public overall.

This page, from the Pew Research Center, presents findings on Hispanics' views regarding key national issues. It highlights that while most Hispanics support legal abortion in all or most cases, opinions vary by religious and age groups. Hispanics are also more likely than the general public to favor controlling gun ownership. The text notes that these attitudes follow recent Supreme Court decisions that restricted access to legal abortions and expanded rights to carry guns in public. Additionally, a majority of Hispanics consider creating a path to legal status for immigrants who arrived illegally as children to be a very important policy goal, a stance held by a greater share than the overall U.S. public.

**Text Evidence:**
- Most Hispanics say abortion should be legal in all or most cases.
- Views on abortion vary across religious and age groups.
- Hispanics favor controlling gun ownership at higher rates than the general public.
- Recent Supreme Court decisions resulted in restricted access to legal abortions and expanded rights to carry guns in public.
- A majority of Hispanics say it is a very important policy goal to create a path to legal status for immigrants who arrived illegally to the U.S. as children.
- This view is held by a greater share among Hispanics than among the U.S. public overall.

The main content is a horizontal bar chart that displays the percentage of Latinos who consider various immigration goals to be "very important," broken down by political party (Democratic/Lean Dem and Republican/Lean Rep). The text provides key statistics from the chart, highlighting that younger Latinos (74% of ages 18-29) are more likely to support maintaining home-country customs, while older Latinos (55% of ages 65+) are more likely to support adopting American customs. It also notes that U.S.-born and second-generation Latinos are more supportive of allowing immigrants to maintain their customs than Latino immigrants.

**Text Evidence:**
- Latino immigrants (40%) are about as likely as U.S.-born Latinos (34%) to say immigrants should adopt American customs.
- U.S.-born Latinos (63%) and second-generation Latinos (67%) are more likely than Latino immigrants (54%) to say immigrants should be allowed to maintain their unique customs.
- Nearly three-quarters of Latinos ages 18 to 29 (74%) say immigrants in the U.S. should be able to hold on to the customs of their home country.
- About half of Latinos ages 65 or older (55%) say immigrants in the U.S. should adopt American customs.
- Latinos with at least a bachelor's degree (66%) are more likely than those with a high school education or less (55%) to say immigrants should be able to hold on to their unique customs.
- Source: National Survey of Latinos conducted Aug. 1-14, 2022.

About half of Latino voters say they plan to vote for the Democratic candidate in their district's election for the U.S. House of Representatives;  $28\%$  say they plan to vote for the Republican candidate, and  $18\%$  are either not sure who they will vote for or plan to support another candidate. Eight-in-ten Hispanic registered voters (80%) say the economy is very important in making their decision about who to vote for in the 2022 congressional elections. Health care (71%), education (70%), violent crime (70%) and gun policy (66%) are the next most cited issues. Meanwhile, half or more of Hispanic voters say abortion (57%) and immigration (54%) are very important to their vote in the midterm elections this year.

Abortion has risen in importance as a voting issue for Hispanics who are registered to vote since the spring: It rose from  $42\%$  in March to  $57\%$  in August. The increase is driven primarily by Hispanic Democrats and Democratic leaners registered to vote (42% in March and 63% in August). By comparison, the share of Hispanic Republicans and Republican leaners registered to vote who say abortion is a very important voting issue has remained relatively flat (43% in March vs. 48% in August).

The main finding is that Latino Republican registered voters are significantly more likely than their Democratic and independent counterparts to have given a lot of thought to the upcoming congressional elections. - Among Latino registered voter Democrats and Latino independents who lean Democratic, more liberals (36%) than conservatives and moderates (21%) say they have given a lot of thought to the elections.

The main finding is that younger Latinos (ages 18-29) are significantly more likely than older Latinos to view social changes as generally good for society. This page from the Pew Research Center presents data on Hispanic attitudes toward socialism in the U.S., based on a national survey conducted August 1-14, 2022. The main finding is that Cubans are significantly more likely than other Hispanic groups to have a negative impression of socialism, with 82% reporting a "somewhat" or "very negative" view compared to 16% who have a positive view. In contrast, Central Americans (47%) and Mexicans (43%) are more likely to hold a positive impression. The information is presented in a two-part dot plot chart showing the percentage of respondents with negative and positive impressions across different Hispanic origin groups.

**Text Evidence:**
- 82% of Cubans have a very or somewhat negative impression of socialism.
- 64% of Puerto Ricans, 51% of Mexicans, and 42% of Central Americans have a negative impression.
- 16% of Cubans have a positive impression of socialism.
- 47% of Central Americans and 43% of Mexicans have a positive impression.
- The data is from the National Survey of Latinos conducted Aug. 1-14, 2022.

Methodology The American Trends Panel survey methodology Overview The American Trends Panel (ATP), created by Pew Research Center, is a nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults. Panelists participate via self-administered web surveys. Panelists who do not have internet access at home are provided with a tablet and wireless internet connection. Interviews are conducted in both English and Spanish. The panel is being managed by Ipsos. Data in this report is drawn from the panel wave conducted from Aug. 1-14, 2022, and included oversamples of Hispanic, Asian and Black adults, as well as 18- to 29-year-old Republicans and Republican-leaning independents in order to provide more precise estimates of the opinions and experiences of these smaller demographic subgroups. These oversampled groups are weighted back to reflect their correct proportions in the population. A total of 7,647 panelists responded out of 13,221 who were sampled, for a response rate of  $65\%$ . This included 6,025 respondents from the ATP and an oversample of 1,622 Hispanic respondents from Ipsos' KnowledgePanel. The cumulative response rate accounting for nonresponse to the recruitment surveys and attrition is  $3\%$ . The break-off rate among panelists who logged on to the survey and completed at least one item is  $2 \%$ The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 7,647 respondents is plus or minus 1.7 percentage points. Panel recruitment The ATP was created in 2014, with the first cohort of panelists invited to join the panel at the end of a large, national, landline and cellphone random-digit-dial survey that was conducted in both English and Spanish. Two additional recruitments were conducted using the same method in 2015 and 2017,

Questionnaire development and testing

The questionnaire was developed by Pew Research Center in consultation with Ipsos. The web program was rigorously tested on both PC and mobile devices by the Ipsos project management team and Pew Research Center researchers. The Ipsos project management team also populated test data that was analyzed in SPSS to ensure the logic and randomizations were working as intended before launching the survey.
Incentives

All respondents were offered a post-paid incentive for their participation. Respondents could choose to receive the post-paid incentive in the form of a check or a gift code to Amazon.com or could choose to decline the incentive. Incentive amounts ranged from  $5 to$ 20 depending on whether the respondent belongs to a part of the population that is harder or easier to reach. Differential incentive amounts were designed to increase panel survey participation among groups that traditionally have low survey response propensities.

Ipsos operates an ongoing modest incentive program for KnowledgePanel to encourage participation and create member loyalty. The incentive program includes special raffles and sweepstakes with both cash rewards and other prizes to be won. Typically, panel members are assigned no more than one survey per week. On average, panel members complete two to three surveys per month with durations of 10 to 15 minutes per survey. An additional incentive is usually provided for longer surveys. For this survey, during the last few days of data collection, KnowledgePanel members were offered 10,000 points (equivalent to $10) in addition to the regular incentive program in an attempt to boost the number of responses from panel members of Central American ancestry.

This does not pose a problem for most of the variables used in the weighting, which are quite stable at both the population and individual levels. However, volunteerism may have changed over the intervening period in ways that made these more recent measurements incompatible with the available (pre-pandemic) benchmarks. To address this, volunteerism is weighted to an estimated benchmark that attempts to account for possible changes in behavior. The weighting parameter is estimated using the volunteerism profile variable that was measured on the full American Trends Panel in 2021 but weighted using the profile variable that was measured in 2020. For all other weighting dimensions, the more recent panelist measurements were used. For American Trends panelists recruited in 2021, the 2020 volunteerism measure was imputed using data from existing panelists with similar characteristics. This ensures that any patterns of change that were observed in the existing panelists were also reflected in the new recruits when the weighting was performed. pages.ocr_text: Adjusting income and defining income tiers CORRECTION (Jan. 30, 2023): A previous version of this methodology misstated the percentages of Hispanic respondents in each adjusted income tier. These changes do not alter any findings in Pew Research Center reports and analyses that used this data. Family income data reported in this study is adjusted for household size and cost-of-living differences by geography using a similar methodology to Pew Research Center's previous work on the American middle class. The income tiers used in this analysis are also created following methodology previously used in the Center's work on the middle class. Prior to these adjustments, American Trends Panel members were assigned to the midpoint of the income range they selected during the survey to provide an exact income figure for adjustment. The metropolitan area cost-of-living adjustment is based on price indexes published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. These indexes, known as Regional Price Parities (RPP), compare the prices of goods and services across 384 metropolitan statistical areas as well as non-metro areas with the national average prices for the same goods and services. The most recent available data is from 2020. The national estimates presented in the analysis encompass the U.S. adult population. Those who fall outside of the 381 metropolitan statistical areas in which current ATP panelists reside are assigned the RPP for their state's non-metropolitan area. Family incomes are then adjusted for the number of people in a household using the methodology from Pew Research Center's previous work on the American middle class. That is done because a four-person household with an income of say, $50,000, faces a tighter budget constraint than a two-person household with the same income. “Middle-income” adults are in families with annual incomes that are two-thirds to double the median family income in the full ATP sample after incomes have been adjusted for household size and the local cost of living. The median family income for the panel is roughly  $65,800 for an average family of three. Using this median income, the middle-income range is about$ 43,800 to $131,500 annually for a three-person family. Lower-income families have incomes less than roughly $43,800 and upper-income families have incomes greater than roughly $131,500 (all figures expressed in 2021 dollars). CORRECTION (Jan. 30, 2023): A previous version of this methodology misstated the percentages of Hispanic respondents in each adjusted income tier. These changes do not alter any findings in Pew Research Center reports and analyses that used this data.

Family income data reported in this study is adjusted for household size and cost-of-living differences by geography using a similar methodology to Pew Research Center's previous work on the American middle class. The income tiers used in this analysis are also created following methodology previously used in the Center's work on the middle class.
Prior to these adjustments, American Trends Panel members were assigned to the midpoint of the income range they selected during the survey to provide an exact income figure for adjustment.

The metropolitan area cost-of-living adjustment is based on price indexes published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. These indexes, known as Regional Price Parities (RPP), compare the prices of goods and services across 384 metropolitan statistical areas as well as non-metro areas with the national average prices for the same goods and services. The most recent available data is from 2020.

The national estimates presented in the analysis encompass the U.S. adult population. Those who fall outside of the 381 metropolitan statistical areas in which current ATP panelists reside are assigned the RPP for their state's non-metropolitan area.

Family incomes are then adjusted for the number of people in a household using the methodology from Pew Research Center's previous work on the American middle class. That is done because a four-person household with an income of say, $50,000, faces a tighter budget constraint than a two-person household with the same income.

“Middle-income” adults are in families with annual incomes that are two-thirds to double the median family income in the full ATP sample after incomes have been adjusted for household size and the local cost of living. The median family income for the panel is roughly  $65,800 for an average family of three. Using this median income, the middle-income range is about$ 43,800 to $131,500 annually for a three-person family. Lower-income families have incomes less than roughly $43,800 and upper-income families have incomes greater than roughly $131,500 (all figures expressed in 2021 dollars).

Based on these adjustments,  $50\%$  of Hispanic respondents in Wave 113 are lower income,  $37\%$  are middle income and  $8\%$  fall into the upper-income tier. An additional  $5\%$  either didn't offer a response to the income question or the household size question. Two examples of how a given area's cost-of-living adjustment was calculated are as follows: the Florence-Muscle Shoals metropolitan area in Alabama is a relatively inexpensive area, with a price level that is  $17.6\%$  less than the national average. The San Francisco-Oakland-Berkeley metropolitan area in California is one of the most expensive areas, with a price level that is  $17.4\%$  higher than the national average.
